1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Thessalonians are Macedonians. These, having received the word of truth in Christ Jesus, persevered in the faith, even in the persecution of their own citizens. Moreover, they did not receive false apostles, nor what was said by false apostles. The Apostle praises them, writing to them from Athens, by Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte. Silvanus and Timothy. The greeting is prefixed with their names, but the sense and words of this epistle are those of the apostle alone.
1.2: 1.2 Grace to you and peace. In his custom he sends a greeting first, and after it gives thanks for their good qualities, recalling not only faith and works, but also the manner of their conversion and their endurance of evils.
1.3: 1.3 Before God. Hence so certain as if you already saw, and so he encourages them.
1.5: 1.5 In the Holy Spirit. Because through me you received the gifts of the Spirit, not sparingly but in fullness. What manner of men we were, etc. By this also, that we suffered as an example to you, it is plain that God loved and chose you.
2.1: 2.1 For not. You know this about it, that it was not in worldly prosperity, which is empty, but in much anxiety amid adversities: and for that reason we had confidence not in ourselves, who are frail, but in the Lord.
2.2: 2.2 At Philippi. The distress he mentions here he suffered on account of the spirit of Python, which he had cast out of the girl.
2.3: 2.3 The exhortation. Here he seems to begin against the false apostles, recalling the truth of the Gospel, then his own prudent conduct among us. In guile. Even truth is in guile when it is preached not for love of truth and the benefit of the hearers, but to gain glory or some other profit.
2.4: 2.4 Not as pleasing men. Unless he himself works in us, we cannot avoid this. For what powers of harm the love of human glory has, only he feels who has declared war on it: because although it is easy for anyone not to desire praise while it is denied, it is hard not to be delighted by it when it is offered.
2.5: 2.5 Neither. In this he touches the false apostles, who wished themselves rather than the teaching of God to be commended. The Apostle, however, who sought glory not for the present but in the future, made himself humble that the preaching of God might be exalted. In occasion. I do not say in avarice, but I neither did nor said anything in which there might be occasion for avarice. Hence it is. God is witness, who knows the heart: for this is not so plain to men.
2.7: 2.7 We could, etc. He so weighs against the cause of the false apostles that he says he refused, though he might have sought support to restrain those who had neither means nor shame in asking. The due of apostolic power he calls a burden, because of the false apostles, who, usurping it unduly, importunately exacted it from the people. His own children. A woman sometimes nurses another's children for pay, not from love: but her own, from affection.
2.12: 2.12 He called, with the calling which is according to purpose.
2.13: 2.13 Therefore. Because he called you, we give thanks. I say he called, which appears from this, that you quickly and firmly received the word, etc. The hearing of God. That is, what we heard from God, or in which God is heard. As it is the word of God. For they received the word with such devotion that they proved they had understood it to be the teaching of God.
2.14: 2.14 For you became imitators, etc. He has said much against the false apostles: now he exhorts them not to be moved by his own or the apostles' tribulation.
2.16: 2.16 Is come. They always fill up their sins, therefore, because the wrath of God has come upon them to blind them. To the end. Because at the end of the age some of the Jews will be converted. In mouth, in sight, etc. Mouth and sight were absent, because the Apostle could not speak to them face to face; but the heart and the anxiety do not rest.
2.18: 2.18 But hindered. That God permitted it to be hindered is for a greater crown for these, because they stood in his absence.
2.19: 2.19 What is, etc. Chrysostom: How great is this ardor! Never, if father and mother had come together and mingled their longing, could they have shown a longing equal to Paul's. I rejoice, he says, more for you than for a crown. Think, then, how great it is for the Church to be present entire, which was planted by Paul and took root. Or the crown of glory. If it is glory now, what will it be before the true judge?
3.2: 3.2 To strengthen you. For this he himself had desired to come.
3.6: 3.6 As we also you: therefore. Because he announced these things, we were comforted, not on account of his presence.
3.9: 3.9 For what thanks, etc. For nothing is so worthy that it could suffice to compensate for the salvation acquired by the nations.
3.13: 3.13 Without blame. That you may not complain of evils, or be so innocent that no one can complain of you, and that you may be also. In holiness. That is, in the consummation of virtues, being by this before God, not in the sight of men.
4.1: 4.1 For the rest. Up to now he persuaded the perfect to patience in their own or others' tribulation; now he persuades the lesser of cleanness, exhorting them to continence. As. By hearing and understanding from us, that is, from me and Silvanus. How you ought to walk, etc., so also walk, living rightly. And to please God. He pleases God who adorns the right faith he has with the carrying out of virtues and perfect action. So also walk. The order is: we ask that you walk as you have received. That you may abound the more. This is not changed in the order of the text.
4.2: 4.2 For you know what precepts. Jerome: Sanctification calls the Christian back from all incontinence, for whom, being incontinent, it does not profit to touch the holy body of Christ, especially since Moses, wishing to sanctify the Jews, commanded the whole people to abstain from every woman, that they might deserve to obtain the presence of God.
4.4: 4.4 His vessel. That is, his wife, let him possess by ruling her, and this, In sanctification, abstaining from intercourse on feast days, In honor. Not abusing her shamefully.
4.8: 4.8 Who also gave, etc. To accomplish these things he gave you the Spirit, so do not despise so great a helper, who does not dwell in a body subject to sins. Or to us apostles, that the authority of preaching and reproving might be greater. But we beseech you, brethren, etc. The exhortation is not contrary to the aforesaid laws. For it happened that some supplied the needy liberally, while others, because of their munificence, neglected to work. Rightly, then, he both praised those and gave useful counsel to these.
4.11: 4.11 Give diligence. As if to say: It is hard to give up a habit, but force yourselves. And work with your hands. Work is to be done, not idling: because it is both honorable, and as a light to unbelievers, and you will not covet another's property, much less beg or take it.
4.12: 4.12 We would not. After the exhortation on continence, and after the correction of curiosity, he confirms that the dead will rise, both through the resurrection of Christ and by his own authority.
4.13: 4.13 Through Jesus will bring with him. Always going, following him, they came to the sleep of death, whence it is written in the other Epistle: We who live.
4.14: 4.14 Them. Not only those who will be found alive, but also the dead, about whom you doubt. Who have slept. He says Christ dead, the faithful sleeping, that they may believe the resurrection the more: he calls Christ dead, that while we hear that he died and rose, we too may hope to rise by the power of his divinity.
4.15: 4.15 For the Lord himself. In his own person. With the trumpet of God. Anselm: This trumpet will rouse all and terrify enemies, will invite his own to war, that they may overcome adversaries, and that they flee from the face of the Lord and be sent into Gehenna. And again, as the trumpet once summoned the people of the Hebrews on feasts: so this trumpet will summon the people of the saints to the solemnity of eternal joy, he says, at God's command and the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God sounding. He shall descend. Not humble as before, but commanding by voice, either of himself or of the archangel, or of the angels, by which he will make the dead rise, which is called a trumpet, because manifest, or as for battle, which will be of God and of Christ, to whom God will give efficacy.
4.16: 4.16 In the clouds. Because a cloud will receive them, as it received Christ at the ascension, whence another translator says: the clouds bearing them.
5.1: 5.1 Of the times. That is, whether in summer or winter, by day or night. And moments. Namely, at what hour of day or night Christ will come.
5.2: 5.2 The day of the Lord. This day is men's at their own pleasure, but then it will be the day of the Lord. As a thief. So unforeseen will he come to the wicked then, as also happens at the death of each. As a thief, I do not say by day but by night, when he comes more secretly and men sleep, then he steals everything: so that he who thought himself rich, awaking, finds nothing. So many who are secure here will then find they have nothing good. For this reason he began with the times, to admonish them to beware, lest they be caught so.
5.3: 5.3 For when they shall say. For as is found in the words of Daniel: Antichrist and his ministers will reign three years and a half, and Elijah and Enoch will be killed by him, as it is also in the Apocalypse: And then there will be such tribulation as was not before, nor will be after. Afterward he will be killed by Michael with the greatest part of his followers.
5.5: 5.5 Children of light. Faith is the light that makes the day, that is, the habit of virtues; on the contrary, darkness is unbelief, night the habit of vices. We are not of the night nor of darkness, etc. That is, in present things let us not grow sluggish, but let the mind be watchful, attending to these perishable things, and let us use them soberly, not as our goods but as given for sustenance. Truly we who are not of the night ought not to sleep. For he who sleeps sleeps because of the night, that is, their vices and sins have drawn them to this, that, forgetting eternal life, they rest in these things, and those who are drunk, by using them immoderately; they have this from the night of vices. Having put on the breastplate, etc. As a breastplate protects the vitals, so faith and charity protect us against the appetite for earthly things.
5.13: 5.13 That you have them. By ministering necessities to them, and showing reverence to their dignity. For what does it profit to have honor without fruit? As riches beget neglect of salvation, so want, while it seeks to be satisfied, turns aside from justice. Therefore in another epistle he commands that priests be held worthy of double honor.
5.15: 5.15 Evil for evil. Then evil is rendered for evil, if one who ought to be corrected is not corrected, but is neglected by perverse dissimulation. Toward all, etc. Generally to all. Without ceasing. That is, always live justly and desire eternal things. The just man never ceases to pray unless he ceases to be just. He prays always who always does well. For the good desire itself is prayer; and if the desire is continual, the prayer is continual.
5.18: 5.18 In Christ. The will of God is shown, because these things were in Christ, in whom nothing displeased God. Do not quench the Spirit. Because it is the will of God to do all these things, you elders who have through the Holy Spirit the gift of understanding, do not hide it, by which merit you too would lose it. You subjects, do not despise their prophecies, yet do not accept all indiscriminately, but prove, that is, examine by reason, and hold what is found good. Do not quench the Spirit, that is: If the Holy Spirit reveals something into someone's ear, do not forbid him to speak what he perceives. The Holy Spirit who has been given to us, not as to himself but in us, we quench when by sinning we drive him away.
5.23: 5.23 And may the God of peace himself sanctify you in all things, etc. That is, I thus admonish prelates and subjects, but God himself is the one who can. Your spirit. Let reason be kept whole, not consenting to the flesh. And soul. That is, let sensuality be kept whole, by serving reason. And body. That you do nothing by its ministry of which anyone may complain. Sometimes the soul is stained by an evil thought and yet the body is clean. And therefore he says the spirit ought to be whole in man. But if an evil life or thought intervene, it will not be spirit. Spirit and soul and body, of which man consists, namely that by which we understand, and that by which we live, and that by which we are visible and tangible, which two are again spoken of, because often the soul is named with the spirit. Without blame. It is one thing to be without sin, which in this life is said of the Only-begotten alone. It is another to be without blame, which could be said of many just men even in this life. Because there is a certain measure of good life, concerning which even in this conduct no just complaint can be made. At the coming. That is, to the end of life.
5.24: 5.24 Faithful. As if to say: I pray that he sanctify, that he keep the sanctified, and one must not doubt this, because he is true in his promises, who called you to this, that you might be holy.
